name: ADOX CHS 100 II
description: Classic cubic-grain B&W film with a traditional, old-school look and genuine German craftsmanship. Warm, slightly vintage tonal quality. Handles well in a wide range of developers.
history: Traces lineage to the original ADOX KB-14 and KB-17 films from the 1950s. 'CHS' stands for Cubic-grain, High Silver-content. Manufactured in Bad Saarow using traditional coating techniques.
shooting_tips: Responds beautifully to Rodinal for a classic European look. Rate at ISO 80 for smoother tones. Warm tonal base prints beautifully on fiber papers. ADOX Adolux ATM 49 produces finest grain.
grain: Medium-fine cubic grain with classic character
contrast: Medium with gentle, traditional tonal curve
latitude: Moderate -- about 1.5 stops
color_palette: Warm silver tones with slightly brownish base

name: ADOX CMS 20 II
description: Officially the highest-resolution film in the world, resolving over 800 line pairs per millimeter. Virtually grainless even under extreme magnification. In ADOTECH developer, achieves continuous-tone; in standard developers, produces near-lithographic contrast.
history: Derived from microfilm and document-copying emulsion technology. Holds the distinction of being the world's highest-resolution pictorial photographic film. ADOX created the dedicated ADOTECH developer specifically for this stock.
shooting_tips: ADOTECH developer is essential for continuous-tone results. Demands the best optics you own -- ruthlessly reveals lens softness. Sturdy tripod and cable release mandatory. Bracket in half-stop increments.
grain: Virtually nonexistent -- finest-grained pictorial film ever produced
contrast: Ultra-high in standard developers; medium in ADOTECH
latitude: Very narrow -- about half a stop; precise exposure critical
color_palette: Clean, neutral silver tones with pristine whites and deep blacks

name: ADOX Color Mission 200
description: ADOX's entry into the color film market. Distinctive European color rendering with natural, slightly muted colors and fine grain. Leans toward restrained, realistic tones rather than heavy saturation.
history: A significant milestone for ADOX, historically known exclusively for B&W. Signals ADOX's ambitions to become a full-spectrum film manufacturer. Positioned as an alternative to heavily saturated color films.
shooting_tips: Overexpose by half to one stop for richest colors and smoothest grain. The restrained palette works beautifully for portraits and travel. Process in standard C-41.
grain: Fine with smooth, organic texture
contrast: Medium with natural, balanced tonal curve
latitude: Good -- about 2 stops, especially toward overexposure
color_palette: Natural, slightly muted with warm skin tones and honest blues

name: ADOX HR-50
description: High-resolution B&W film delivering exceptional sharpness at a practical ISO 50 speed. Sits between the extreme CMS 20 II and traditional CHS 100 II, offering high resolution without requiring specialty developers.
history: Developed as a more accessible high-resolution option than CMS 20 II. 'HR' stands for High Resolution. Delivers significantly more resolving power than standard ISO 50-100 films while working with standard developers.
shooting_tips: Unlike CMS 20 II, produces excellent results in standard developers like D-76, XTOL, and Rodinal. Rate at box speed for best grain/resolution balance. Quality optics make the most of this film's resolution.
grain: Very fine with high acutance
contrast: Medium with clean, modern tonal curve
latitude: Moderate -- about 1.5 stops; more forgiving than CMS 20 II
color_palette: Neutral, clean silver tones with precise separation

name: ADOX Silvermax 100
description: Unique B&W film containing ~70% more silver than conventional films, producing up to 14 zones of dynamic range when developed in ADOX's dedicated Silvermax developer. Extraordinary tonal depth and three-dimensional print quality.
history: Developed by ADOX in Bad Saarow, Germany as a showcase for what's possible when silver content constraints are relaxed. One of the most expensive films to manufacture per frame.
shooting_tips: Use ADOX Silvermax developer for the full 14-zone tonal range. Expose at box speed or overexpose by half a stop. Dense negatives may require longer printing exposures. Use a spot meter for best results.
grain: Fine, tightly packed grain in dense silver matrix
contrast: Medium with extraordinarily long tonal scale -- up to 14 zones
latitude: Exceptional -- 3+ stops with Silvermax developer
color_palette: Deep, rich silver tones with luminous highlights and detailed shadows

name: Agfa APX 100
description: Fine-grain panchromatic B&W film continuing the legacy of Agfa's classic emulsions. High resolution and crisp detail with a traditional tonal rendering that many find warmer than comparable Ilford or Kodak films.
history: The APX line traces its origins to the original Agfa-Gevaert company. After Agfa Photo's 2005 bankruptcy, the brand was licensed and production continued. One of the most affordable fine-grain films available.
shooting_tips: Best at box speed in bright, contrasty light. Develops well in Rodinal at high dilutions for stand development. Try rating at ISO 50 and pulling for ultra-smooth gradation.
grain: Very fine with high resolving power
contrast: Medium with smooth, classic tonal curve
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops, prefers accurate exposure
color_palette: Neutral to slightly warm B&W rendering

name: Agfa APX 400
description: Versatile B&W film with classic European tonal character and moderate grain. Grittier and more characterful than APX 100. An affordable alternative to HP5 Plus and Tri-X with its own distinct personality.
history: Shares APX 100's lineage from the original Agfa-Gevaert empire. During the Cold War, Agfa films were the primary stock in West Germany. Positioned as an affordable alternative with character.
shooting_tips: Performs well at box speed. Pushes to 800 with modest grain increase. Rate at ISO 320 for smoother tonality. Rodinal at 1:25 for punchy look, D-76 for smoother results.
grain: Moderate, clearly visible with classic texture
latitude: Good -- about 3 stops, handles overexposure better
color_palette: Classic B&W with slightly cool shadow tones

name: Agfa Vista Plus 200
description: Popular budget color negative film known for warm, saturated colors. Widely understood to be a rebadged Fujifilm emulsion. Though discontinued, it retains a strong cult following and expired rolls command premium prices.
history: Sold under the Agfa brand but was likely a rebadged Fujicolor C200. One of the most widely available consumer films in European supermarkets throughout the 2000s-2010s. Discontinued as AgfaPhoto rationalized its lineup.
shooting_tips: When shooting expired rolls, overexpose by one stop per decade past expiration. The warm rendering is excellent for golden hour. Shoot in direct sunlight for the most saturated colors. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Fine to moderate, smooth in good light
contrast: Medium with gentle, pleasing tonal curve
latitude: Good -- about 3 stops, very forgiving
color_palette: Warm, saturated with vivid greens, golden skin tones

name: Bergger Pancro 400
description: French artisan B&W film with a unique dual-emulsion structure using both silver bromide and silver iodide crystals. Produces exceptionally rich tonal gradation with creamy, luminous shadow rendering. Prized for portraiture and fine art.
history: Developed by Bergger in France as their flagship film stock. The dual-emulsion design is unusual in modern film manufacturing. Available in 35mm, 120, and large format.
shooting_tips: Truly shines when overexposed by half to one stop, enhancing its creamy tonality. In PMK Pyro developer, produces maximum tonal richness. Also works well in D-76 and DDX.
grain: Fine to moderate with smooth, organic structure
contrast: Medium with exceptionally smooth tonal transitions
latitude: Wide -- approximately 4 stops, responds beautifully to generous exposure
color_palette: Warm-leaning B&W with creamy highlights and deep, luminous shadows

name: CineStill 400D
description: CineStill's versatile daylight-balanced film, derived from Kodak Vision3 250D rated at 400 ISO. Bridges the gap between the fine-grained 50D and high-speed 800T, offering practical all-around speed with cinematic color rendering.
history: Released in 2022 after a successful crowdfunding campaign, 400D filled the major gap in CineStill's lineup. Based on Vision3 250D (5207) but rated at 400 to account for remjet removal.
shooting_tips: Versatile from bright daylight to shade. Overexpose by 1 stop for softer, warmer tones. Under tungsten light, expect a warm orange shift. Can be pushed to 800. Processes in standard C-41.
grain: Fine to medium -- finer than typical 400-speed consumer films
latitude: Very good -- benefits from cinema stock's wide dynamic range
color_palette: Natural, slightly warm daylight colors with cinematic rendering

name: CineStill 50D
description: CineStill's daylight-balanced film, derived from Kodak Vision3 50D motion picture stock. Delivers incredibly fine grain, rich saturation, and a clean, cinematic color palette optimized for daylight shooting.
history: Launched as CineStill's daytime counterpart to 800T. The remjet anti-halation layer is removed, which can produce halation around bright highlights, though less pronounced than on 800T.
shooting_tips: Best in bright daylight and golden hour. Low ISO demands good lighting or a tripod. Under tungsten light, use an 80A filter or embrace the warm shift. Processes in standard C-41.
grain: Extremely fine -- finest grain of any CineStill stock
latitude: Very good -- cinema film heritage provides excellent latitude
color_palette: Clean, accurate daylight colors with rich saturation and cinematic quality

name: CineStill 800T
description: Kodak Vision3 500T motion picture film, adapted for still photography. CineStill 800T is tungsten-balanced, meaning it renders warm artificial light as neutral while giving daylight scenes a cool, blue cast. Its signature feature is the 'halation', a red/orange glow around highlights caused by the removal of the remjet anti-halation layer.
history: CineStill was founded in 2012 by brothers Brian and Brandon Wright, who developed a process to remove the remjet backing from Kodak Vision3 motion picture film, making it processable in standard C-41 chemistry. The 800T (based on Vision3 500T, rated at 800) quickly became one of the most popular and recognizable film stocks of the modern era, defining the look of urban night photography.
shooting_tips: Best at night under artificial light -- neon signs, street lamps, and city lights produce the most stunning results. The halation (red glow around bright highlights) is the defining characteristic and cannot be avoided. Use an 85B warming filter in daylight to correct the blue cast, or embrace it for a cinematic cool look. Can be pushed to 1600 or 3200 for even lower light. Meter for shadows to retain the atmospheric mood.
grain: Medium
latitude: Good -- cinema film stock heritage gives good shadow detail
color_palette: Tungsten-balanced: warm lights rendered neutral, cool daylight; red halation around highlights

name: CineStill BwXX
description: CineStill's B&W film, derived from Kodak Eastman Double-X 5222 with the remjet removed for standard processing. Delivers the classic Hollywood B&W cinematic look with rich midtones, deep blacks, and smooth, filmic grain.
history: Brings cinema's most storied B&W emulsion to still photographers in an easy-to-process format. Unlike original Double-X, no special remjet removal step is needed -- develops in any standard B&W developer.
shooting_tips: Rate at 200-250 for daylight, push to 400-800 for indoor work. D-76 and HC-110 produce classic results. Pushes cleanly with increasing contrast and grain. Distinctive cinematic tonal curve.
grain: Medium -- classic, filmic grain with a cinematic quality
contrast: Low to medium -- smooth cinematic tonal curve
latitude: Very good -- wide dynamic range from motion picture heritage
color_palette: Rich midtones, velvety blacks, smooth highlight transitions

name: Dubblefilm Monsoon
description: Pre-exposed color negative film producing cool blue and teal effects. Atmospheric images with aquatic, moody overlays evoking rain, ocean, and twilight moods.
history: Introduced as the cool-toned counterpart to Sunstroke. Hand-pre-exposed at Dubblefilm's Barcelona studio using controlled blue and teal light sources.
shooting_tips: Works beautifully in overcast, rainy, or twilight conditions. Cool-toned subjects harmonize with the blue overlay. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Fine to moderate from ISO 200 base stock
contrast: Medium, slightly muted by cool overlay
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Cool blue, teal, and cyan washes with moody undertones

name: Dubblefilm Sunstroke
description: Pre-exposed color negative film producing warm, golden light leak effects on every frame. Orange and amber washes blend with the photographer's exposures for dreamy, sun-drenched images.
history: One of Dubblefilm's original offerings, created at their Barcelona studio where each roll is pre-exposed by hand. Quickly became their flagship product.
shooting_tips: Shoot in bright daylight. Slight overexposure helps the warm effects blend. Avoid very dark scenes. Each frame is unique. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Fine to moderate from ISO 200 base stock
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops, best with generous exposure
color_palette: Golden, amber, and orange light leak washes

name: Film Ferrania P30 Alpha
description: Panchromatic B&W film reviving the spirit of classic Italian cinema emulsions. Beautifully rich, deep blacks and smooth tonal gradation with a cinematic quality reminiscent of Italian neorealist films. A creamy, luminous midtone rendering uniquely its own.
history: Flagship product of the revived Film Ferrania, which raised over $300,000 through Kickstarter in 2014. The 'P30' connects to Ferrania's classic motion picture film. Production has been limited as the small team scales up.
shooting_tips: ISO 80 requires good light or a tripod. Look for scenes with strong shadow areas for the signature deep blacks. Develops beautifully in D-96 or D-76. Rodinal at 1:50 for enhanced sharpness.
grain: Fine, smooth grain with creamy, organic texture
contrast: Medium-high with exceptionally deep, rich blacks
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops, slightly better overexposed
color_palette: Rich, deep blacks with creamy midtones -- distinctly Italian cinematic aesthetic

name: Film Washi A
description: Photographic film coated on genuine Japanese Washi paper. At ISO 12, produces images with a dreamlike, painterly quality where the paper's natural fibers become visible. Each roll is hand-coated -- truly artisanal.
history: Created by Lomig Perrotin of Film Washi in France. The Washi paper base is a traditional Japanese paper prized for centuries in art. One of the rarest and most artisanal film stocks in the world.
shooting_tips: Tripod essential at ISO 12. The paper base creates soft, diffused images. Focus on subjects with strong shapes and high contrast. Handle gently during development -- paper base is more delicate.
grain: No traditional grain; texture dominated by Washi paper fibers
contrast: Low to medium with soft, diffused transitions
latitude: Very narrow -- about 1 stop; precise exposure critical
color_palette: Soft, warm-toned B&W with organic, handmade quality

name: Film Washi S
description: Experimental B&W film made from repurposed sound recording film stock. Orthochromatic emulsion on clear polyester base produces extremely high contrast, graphic images with virtually no grain. Razor-sharp detail.
history: Created using surplus sound recording film designed to capture optical soundtracks on motion picture prints. Its high-resolution audio properties produce striking photographic results.
shooting_tips: Orthochromatic -- not sensitive to red light, so reds render very dark. Works best for graphic, high-contrast subjects. Dilute Rodinal with stand development tames contrast.
grain: Virtually grainless -- glass-smooth images
contrast: Very high -- tends toward stark blacks and whites
latitude: Very narrow -- about 1-2 stops; precise exposure critical
color_palette: Pure, stark B&W with almost lithographic quality

name: Fomapan 100 Classic
description: Traditional cubic-grain B&W film with genuine European character. Moderate grain with warm tonality reminiscent of mid-20th century photography. Good sharpness with a distinctive vintage aesthetic. Available in all major formats and exceptionally affordable.
history: In production at the Foma Bohemia factory in Czech Republic for decades, with roots tracing back to 1921. Uses traditional cubic-grain emulsion technology that preserves authentic vintage character.
shooting_tips: Rate at box speed or pull to ISO 80 for smoothest tones. Rodinal at 1:50 for stand development produces beautiful results. Has a distinctive response to red and orange filters for dramatic skies.
grain: Medium cubic grain with classic, textured look
latitude: Moderate -- about 1.5 stops in either direction
color_palette: Warm-toned silver with slightly brownish midtones

name: Fomapan 200 Creative
description: Medium-speed B&W film occupying the sweet spot between fine grain and versatility. The 'Creative' name reflects its flexibility -- responds well to push and pull processing for contrast and grain control. Excellent all-around film.
history: Part of the Fomapan lineup for decades. The ISO 200 speed point was historically popular in European photography and is a niche few other manufacturers still serve.
shooting_tips: Pushes well to 400, pulls to 100 for smoother results. Rodinal at 1:50 brings out acutance and a classic European look. Ideal for photographers who want one stock for both bright and overcast conditions.
grain: Medium cubic grain with pleasant, organic texture
latitude: Good -- about 2 stops in either direction with push/pull flexibility
color_palette: Neutral to slightly warm silver tones

name: Fomapan 400 Action
description: Fast B&W film with prominent, characterful grain and punchy contrast. A gritty, photojournalistic aesthetic from cubic-grain emulsion. One of the most affordable high-speed B&W films on the market.
history: The high-speed member of the Fomapan family. Has gained worldwide following among budget-conscious photographers who appreciate its raw, unpolished aesthetic.
shooting_tips: Many photographers rate it at ISO 200-320 for better shadow detail. Pushes aggressively to 800-1600 for very gritty results. HC-110 Dilution B tames contrast, XTOL at 1:1 gives smoothest results at box speed.
grain: Prominent, chunky cubic grain with raw texture
latitude: Good especially toward overexposure
color_palette: Cool-toned silver with gritty midtones

name: Fomapan R 100
description: One of the very few B&W reversal (slide) films still in production. Produces positive B&W transparencies for direct projection or lightbox viewing. Blacks are truly black and whites glow with inner light. Requires dedicated reversal chemistry.
history: One of the last remaining B&W reversal films in production anywhere in the world. Used by fine-art photographers, archives, museums, and scientific institutions. A testament to Foma's commitment to preserving photographic traditions.
shooting_tips: Reversal demands precise exposure -- bracket in half-stop increments. Overexposure blows to clear film, underexposure blocks to pure black. Processing requires Foma's dedicated reversal chemistry kit.
grain: Fine, tight grain with exceptional clarity in positive transparencies
contrast: High -- inherent to the reversal process
latitude: Very narrow -- about half a stop tolerance
color_palette: Pure, luminous silver-black tones with exceptional density range

name: Retropan 320 Soft
description: Unique B&W film designed to produce ultra-soft, low-contrast images with a dreamy, pictorialist quality. Deliberately minimizes contrast and sharpness for an ethereal, glowing look evoking early 20th-century art photography.
history: Introduced by Foma as a specialty art film replicating the soft-focus pictorialist aesthetic. Represents Foma's willingness to produce niche, creative products no other manufacturer would consider.
shooting_tips: Embrace the softness -- don't fight it with sharpening. Low-contrast developers enhance the dreamy quality. Backlit subjects produce the most ethereal results. Pairs beautifully with soft-focus lenses and plastic cameras.
grain: Fine but diffuse, contributing to the overall soft quality
contrast: Very low by design -- compressed tonal range
latitude: Good due to soft tonal curve
color_palette: Soft, warm silver tones with gentle highlight glow

name: Fujifilm C200
description: Fujifilm's budget daylight film. C200 delivers muted, slightly desaturated colors with a cool bias. It has a softer, more dreamy quality than Superia, making it popular for casual shooting and lo-fi aesthetics. Extremely affordable where available, it's become a favorite for photographers who want a laid-back, film-y look.
history: C200 has been Fujifilm's most affordable film stock for decades, manufactured primarily for Asian and emerging markets. Its low price point made it a gateway film for many photographers. Availability has become increasingly sporadic as Fujifilm has scaled back film production.
shooting_tips: Best in bright daylight -- this film struggles in low light. Colors are more muted and cooler than Superia. Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother, warmer results. Great for point-and-shoot cameras and casual shooting. Don't expect the saturation of Ektar or the warmth of Kodak -- embrace the softer, cooler Fuji aesthetic.
grain: Medium
latitude: Moderate -- prefers overexposure
color_palette: Cool, soft, slightly muted pastels

name: Fujifilm Natura 1600
description: The holy grail of discontinued film stocks. Natura 1600 was a high-speed color negative film designed for shooting in natural and ambient light without flash. It delivered remarkably natural colors and fine grain for its extreme speed, capturing the warmth of candlelight and neon with intimacy no other film could match.
history: Introduced in 2004 as a companion to Fujifilm's Natura point-and-shoot cameras. Discontinued in 2018, it has become one of the most sought-after expired film stocks, with rolls regularly selling for $50-100+ on the secondary market.
shooting_tips: If you have rolls, shoot at box speed in ambient light for the authentic experience. The film excels under warm artificial light. Don't waste it in bright daylight -- save it for low-light situations. Check expiration dates and keep refrigerated.
grain: Medium -- remarkably fine for 1600 ISO
contrast: Low to medium -- soft, natural rendering
latitude: Good -- designed to handle mixed ambient lighting
color_palette: Warm, natural, intimate -- captures ambient light with remarkable fidelity

name: Fujifilm Neopan Acros II
description: Fujifilm's ultra-fine-grain black and white film, reintroduced by popular demand. Acros II delivers incredibly smooth tonal gradations with virtually no grain, making it ideal for architectural photography, still life, and any situation where maximum detail matters. Its Super Fine Grain technology produces results that rival medium format from a 35mm negative.
history: The original Neopan Acros 100 was discontinued in 2018, causing widespread dismay among B&W film enthusiasts. In response to overwhelming demand, Fujifilm reformulated and reintroduced it as Acros II in 2019, making it one of the few films to be 'un-discontinued.' The new version maintains the character of the original while using updated manufacturing processes.
shooting_tips: Shoot at box speed for finest grain. Handles long exposures exceptionally well with minimal reciprocity failure -- a standout feature for night photography. Develop in Rodinal for more pronounced grain with sharp edges, or in D-76/XTOL for the smoothest possible tones. Meter carefully; this film prefers accurate exposure to overexposure.
grain: Exceptionally fine -- among the finest B&W films
latitude: Good -- but best results at box speed
color_palette: Smooth, creamy tones with excellent highlight and shadow detail

name: Fujifilm Pro 400H
description: A once-beloved professional film known for its unique combination of fine grain, beautiful skin tones, and distinctive cool-green shadow tones. Pro 400H produced a 'clean' look that was highly prized by wedding and portrait photographers. Its discontinuation in 2021 left a void that no other film has fully filled.
history: Introduced in 2004 as Fujifilm's answer to Kodak Portra 400, Pro 400H used Fuji's 4th-color-layer technology for superior color reproduction under various light sources. It became the preferred film for many wedding photographers who wanted a neutral-to-cool alternative to Kodak's warm Portra palette. Fujifilm discontinued it in 2021, devastating its devoted user base.
shooting_tips: If you have rolls stockpiled, overexpose by 1-2 stops for the creamiest, most beautiful results. The characteristic cool green shadow tones are most pronounced when overexposed. Meter for shadows. Absolutely stunning in medium format. This film loved soft, diffused light and shade. Check expiration dates and cold-store any remaining rolls.
grain: Very fine for 400 ISO
latitude: Excellent
color_palette: Neutral with cool green shadow tones, clean pastels

name: Fujifilm Provia 100F
description: Fujifilm's all-purpose professional slide film. Where Velvia is hyper-saturated and dramatic, Provia 100F is balanced, accurate, and versatile. It reproduces colors faithfully with excellent sharpness and fine grain, making it ideal for everything from portraits to landscapes to product photography on slide film.
history: Provia 100F (the F stands for Fine grain) was introduced in 2002 as an update to the original Provia 100. It's positioned as Fujifilm's 'neutral' slide film, sitting between the muted Astia and the saturated Velvia. It remains one of the last professional slide films still in production and is widely used by photographers who want accurate color.
shooting_tips: More forgiving than Velvia but still demands careful metering -- it's slide film, after all. Can be pushed 1-2 stops with good results, unlike Velvia which falls apart when pushed. Great for portraits on slide film due to its accurate, non-exaggerated colors. Use a color meter for critical work. Cross-processing yields more subtle results than Velvia.
grain: Very fine
latitude: Narrow but better than Velvia -- about 1 stop tolerance
color_palette: Accurate, neutral, slightly cool with vivid but natural colors

name: Fujifilm Superia Premium 400
description: Fujifilm's Japan-exclusive premium consumer film, coveted by photographers worldwide for its exceptional color rendering. Delivers finer grain and more refined colors than standard Superia X-TRA 400, with a slightly warmer, more balanced palette.
history: Released exclusively for the Japanese domestic market, its Japan-only status has made it highly sought after internationally, often purchased through importers at a premium. Represents Fujifilm's highest-quality consumer color negative offering.
shooting_tips: Colors are more balanced and natural than standard Superia, with less cool/magenta bias. Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother, warmer results. Import from Japan-based retailers for best pricing. Results scan beautifully.
grain: Fine for a 400-speed consumer film
latitude: Very good -- forgiving of exposure errors
color_palette: Balanced, natural with warm undertones; more refined than standard Superia

name: Fujifilm Superia X-TRA 400
description: Fujifilm's classic consumer film delivers cool-toned, vivid colors with a distinctly 'Fuji' look -- punchy greens, bright blues, and a slightly magenta-biased skin tone. It's the opposite of Kodak's warm rendering, offering a crisp, vibrant aesthetic that many photographers love for street and travel photography.
history: Superia has been Fujifilm's consumer film line since the 1990s, competing directly with Kodak Gold and Ultramax. The X-TRA 400 version has been a staple of drugstore film counters worldwide. As Fuji has discontinued many of their film stocks, Superia remains one of the last affordable Fuji color films available.
shooting_tips: Expect cooler tones than Kodak films -- greens and blues are enhanced, while skin tones lean slightly pink/magenta. Works great for street photography, landscapes, and travel where you want vivid, punchy colors. Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother results. Best in daylight; artificial light can exaggerate the cool color bias.
grain: Medium
latitude: Good
color_palette: Cool, vivid greens and blues, slightly magenta skin tones

name: Fujifilm Velvia 100
description: The more versatile sibling of Velvia 50. Velvia 100 retains the Velvia family's vivid color saturation but with a full stop more speed, slightly finer grain, and a more refined color palette. Saturation is still high but more controlled than Velvia 50.
history: Introduced in 2005 as Velvia 100F, reformulated as Velvia 100 in 2007 with slightly increased saturation. Designed to offer Velvia-level color impact with a more practical ISO speed and better reciprocity for long exposures.
shooting_tips: More forgiving than Velvia 50 but still demands careful metering. The extra stop makes it more practical for handheld shooting. Better for long exposures due to improved reciprocity. Slightly underexpose by 1/3 stop to maximize saturation.
grain: Extremely fine -- slightly finer than Velvia 50
latitude: Narrow -- about 1 stop, slightly better than Velvia 50
color_palette: Vivid, saturated but more refined than Velvia 50; rich greens, blues, and warm tones

name: Fujifilm Velvia 50
description: The king of slide films. Velvia 50 delivers the most vivid, hyper-saturated colors of any film ever made. Landscapes shot on Velvia practically glow -- greens are electric, reds are fiery, and skies are a deep, rich blue. It's a challenging film that rewards careful exposure with images of breathtaking beauty.
history: Launched in 1990, Velvia 50 single-handedly changed landscape photography. It replaced Kodachrome as the slide film of choice for nature photographers, gracing the pages of National Geographic and every landscape photography book of the era. The name comes from 'Velvet Media,' referencing its smooth grain structure. It remains in production and highly sought after.
shooting_tips: Slide film has almost no latitude -- exposure must be precise. Overexposure blows out highlights irretrievably; underexposure by 1/3 stop can actually enhance saturation. Use a spot meter or bracketed exposures. Polarizing filters and graduated ND filters are your best friends. Best in golden hour and overcast light. Avoid shooting in harsh midday sun. Cross-processing in C-41 produces wild, surreal colors.
grain: Extremely fine -- almost invisible
latitude: Very narrow -- 1/2 stop tolerance
color_palette: Ultra-saturated greens, reds, and blues; deep, rich shadows

name: Harman Phoenix 200
description: The first color film ever produced by Harman Technology (Ilford's parent company). Features prominent grain, halation effects, and bold colors leaning heavily into reds and oranges. Embraces imperfection as a creative, lo-fi alternative.
history: Launched in late 2024, a historic first for Harman Technology which had exclusively made B&W materials. The name 'Phoenix' symbolizes color film rising from the ashes. Its single-layer emulsion design produces its characteristically bold, imperfect look.
shooting_tips: Expect strong halation around bright light sources -- use creatively with backlit subjects. Colors are inherently warm with reds dominating. Overexpose by half to one stop for best results. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Prominent, visible grain central to the film's aesthetic
contrast: Medium-high with bold colors and strong halation
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops, better overexposed
color_palette: Bold, warm reds, oranges, yellows with strong halation glow

name: Harman Phoenix II 200
description: The second iteration of Harman's color negative film, Phoenix II builds on the original Phoenix 200 with refinements to grain, halation, and color consistency while retaining the bold, characterful look that made the first version popular.
history: Released after the success of Harman Phoenix 200. Phoenix II offers improved consistency and slightly more controlled halation while keeping the creative, lo-fi aesthetic.
shooting_tips: Similar to Phoenix 200: overexpose by half to one stop. Expect halation around bright lights. Standard C-41. Available in 35mm and 120.
grain: Prominent grain, slightly refined from original Phoenix
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Warm reds and oranges with halation; more controlled than Phoenix 200

name: Harman Red 125
description: Harman Technology's RED is a color negative film with a distinctive red-biased palette. Part of Harman's expanding color film lineup alongside Phoenix and Switch Azure, it offers a creative, saturated look for 35mm and 120 formats.
history: Released by Harman Technology as part of their move into color film. The RED name reflects its pronounced red color cast and bold character.
shooting_tips: Best in daylight. Use the red bias creatively for skin tones and warm scenes. Standard C-41 processing. Available in 35mm and 120.
grain: Moderate grain with saturated color
latitude: Moderate
color_palette: Red-biased, bold and saturated

name: Harman Switch Azure 125
description: Harman Technology's Switch Azure is a color negative film with a cool, azure-blue character. Part of Harman's color film range, it offers a distinct alternative to warm-toned stocks for creative and experimental photography.
history: Released by Harman Technology alongside RED and Phoenix as they expanded into color film production. The 'Switch' line emphasizes alternative color palettes.
shooting_tips: Ideal for cool, moody scenes and overcast light. Standard C-41. Pairs well with blue-hour and aquatic subjects. Available in 35mm and 120.
grain: Moderate grain with cool tone
latitude: Moderate
color_palette: Cool azure, blue-biased with clean highlights

name: Ilford Delta 100
description: Ilford's finest-grained B&W film, built on their Core-Shell tabular grain technology. Delta 100 delivers exceptional sharpness, extremely fine grain, and a wide tonal range with superb detail in both highlights and shadows. Many photographers find it produces richer shadow tones than T-Max 100.
history: Introduced in 1992 as Ilford's answer to Kodak's T-Max line. Uses Ilford's proprietary Core-Shell crystal technology rather than Kodak's T-Grain, producing a tabular-grain film with a distinctly Ilford character.
shooting_tips: Shoot at box speed for finest grain and widest tonal range. Develops beautifully in DD-X, Perceptol, or ID-11. Reciprocity characteristics are excellent for long exposures. Less pushable than Delta 400 or HP5 -- best kept at or near box speed.
grain: Extremely fine -- tabular grain technology
latitude: Good -- best at box speed or slightly overexposed
color_palette: Rich, three-dimensional tones with excellent shadow depth

name: Ilford Delta 3200
description: Ilford's ultra-high-speed B&W film for shooting in near darkness. Delta 3200 uses modern tabular grain technology to deliver usable images at speeds from 1600 to 6400+. The grain is prominent and atmospheric, lending images a raw, documentary quality that's perfect for concerts, nightlife, and street photography after dark.
history: Introduced in 1998 using Ilford's Core-Shell crystal technology, Delta 3200 filled the gap for photographers who needed speed above all else. Its true sensitivity is around ISO 1000-1250, but it's designed to be rated and developed at 3200 for optimal results. It remains one of the few high-speed B&W films in production.
shooting_tips: The true ISO is closer to 1000-1250, so 'box speed' at 3200 is technically a 1.5-stop push. Rating at 1600 gives finer grain and more shadow detail. Pushing to 6400 or even 12500 is possible for extreme situations. Use Ilford DD-X or Microphen developers for best results at high speeds. Embrace the grain -- it's a feature, not a bug.
grain: Prominent -- atmospheric and textural
latitude: Good at rated speed, decreases when pushed further
color_palette: Bold blacks, bright whites, dramatic tonal separation

name: Ilford Delta 400
description: Ilford's modern tabular-grain 400-speed film, bridging the gap between classic HP5 Plus grain and ultra-fine Delta 100. Offers noticeably finer grain than HP5 at the same speed, with a smoother, more modern tonal quality.
history: Launched in 1990 as part of Ilford's Delta tabular-grain family. While HP5 Plus remains more popular for its classic character and pushability, Delta 400 has a loyal following among photographers who prioritize grain smoothness.
shooting_tips: Delivers finest grain at box speed in Perceptol or ID-11. Pushes well to 800 and 1600 in DD-X or Microphen. Overexpose by 1/2 stop for richer shadow detail. Less forgiving of underexposure than HP5 Plus.
grain: Fine -- noticeably finer than HP5 Plus
latitude: Very good -- slightly less than HP5 Plus but still forgiving
color_palette: Smooth, refined tones with gentle gradations and good separation

name: Ilford FP4 Plus
description: Ilford's medium-speed B&W film delivers exceptionally fine grain, beautiful tonality, and superb sharpness. FP4 Plus is the go-to film for landscape, architectural, and studio B&W photography where detail and tonal range are paramount. It rewards careful exposure with images of remarkable clarity.
history: FP4 Plus has been in Ilford's lineup since 1990, succeeding the original FP4. The 'Fine grain Panchromatic' designation reflects its position as Ilford's detail-oriented film. It occupies a similar niche to Kodak's T-Max 100, offering fine grain and high resolution for photographers who shoot in controlled lighting.
shooting_tips: Shoot at box speed or overexpose by 1/2 stop for the richest tonality. Excellent in large format where its fine grain and high resolution truly shine. Develops well in almost any B&W developer -- ID-11/D-76 for classic results, Perceptol for finest grain, or Rodinal for edge sharpness. Pull to ISO 64 for even finer grain in bright conditions.
grain: Very fine
latitude: Good -- handles 1-2 stops of overexposure well
color_palette: Smooth, detailed tones with excellent separation throughout

name: Ilford HP5 Plus
description: Ilford's flagship 400-speed B&W film and Tri-X's eternal rival. HP5 Plus is a traditional cubic-grain film that delivers classic black and white tonality with excellent pushability. It has a slightly softer, more forgiving character than Tri-X, with gentler grain and smoother midtones that many photographers prefer.
history: HP5 Plus traces its lineage back to Ilford's original Hypersensitive Panchromatic plate from 1931. The current 'Plus' version was introduced in 1989 with improved grain and sharpness. The Tri-X vs HP5 debate is one of the oldest in photography, with passionate advocates on both sides. HP5 remains Ilford's best-selling film.
shooting_tips: Pushes beautifully to 800, 1600, and even 3200 -- Ilford's Microphen developer is specially designed for pushing HP5. At box speed, expect smooth grain and a full tonal range. Overexpose by 1 stop for richer shadows. In stand development with Rodinal (1:100 for 1 hour), HP5 produces stunning results with compressed tones and sharp grain.
grain: Medium -- slightly softer than Tri-X
latitude: Excellent -- very forgiving of exposure errors
color_palette: Rich, full tonal range with smooth gradations

name: Ilford Ortho Plus
description: Ilford's orthochromatic B&W film -- not sensitive to red light. Red tones render as dark/black, blue skies appear lighter. The lack of red sensitivity also means it can be handled and developed under a red safelight, making it a unique creative and teaching tool.
history: Introduced in 2019, inspired by orthochromatic emulsions that were standard before panchromatic film became dominant in the early 20th century. Its safelight compatibility makes it popular with darkroom enthusiasts.
shooting_tips: Red subjects render very dark or black -- use creatively. Blue skies appear brighter. Rate at ISO 80 in daylight or ISO 40 under tungsten. Develop under a red safelight for tray processing by inspection.
grain: Fine -- clean, classic grain structure
latitude: Moderate -- meter carefully for best results
color_palette: Unique tonal rendering: dark reds, bright blues, distinctive skin tones

name: Ilford Pan F Plus
description: Ilford's ultra-slow, ultra-fine-grain B&W film for absolute maximum sharpness and detail. Pan F Plus 50 delivers grain so fine it's virtually invisible, with extraordinary resolving power and a beautiful, luminous tonal quality.
history: Pan F has been in Ilford's lineup since 1935, making it one of the oldest continuously available film emulsions. The current 'Plus' version was introduced in 1987. Its name derives from 'Panchromatic Fine grain.'
shooting_tips: Demands bright lighting or a tripod. Develop in Perceptol for finest grain, ID-11 for balance, or Rodinal at high dilution with stand development for unique results. Reciprocity correction needed for exposures over 1 second.
grain: Virtually invisible -- among the finest-grained B&W films made
latitude: Moderate -- demands accurate exposure for best results
color_palette: Luminous, silvery tones with exquisite detail and smooth gradations

name: Ilford SFX 200
description: Ilford's unique near-infrared sensitive B&W film. SFX 200 extends sensitivity into the near-infrared spectrum (up to ~740nm), enabling dramatic infrared-like effects when used with a deep red or IR filter. Foliage glows white, skies turn black, and skin takes on an ethereal quality.
history: Introduced in the 1990s as a more accessible alternative to Kodak's High Speed Infrared film. Unlike Kodak HIE, SFX can be loaded in subdued light. Shot without a filter, it behaves like a conventional panchromatic film.
shooting_tips: Without a filter, it's a normal 200-speed film. For the IR effect, use a deep red filter (Hoya R72) and rate at ISO 25-50. Meter without the filter, then add compensation. Best on sunny days with green foliage for the strongest 'Wood Effect.'
grain: Medium -- slightly coarser than other 200-speed films
contrast: High when used with infrared filters
latitude: Moderate -- tighter with filters due to extreme compensation
color_palette: Dramatic: white foliage, dark skies, ethereal highlights with IR filters

name: Ilford XP2 Super
description: A unique chromogenic B&W film that's processed in standard C-41 color chemistry -- meaning any lab that develops color film can process XP2. It delivers smooth, virtually grainless B&W images with a wide exposure latitude. The C-41 process produces dye clouds instead of silver grain, resulting in an exceptionally smooth tonal quality.
history: XP2 Super evolved from Ilford's original XP1, introduced in 1980 as one of the first chromogenic B&W films. The 'Super' designation was added in 2001. Its ability to be processed in standard C-41 chemistry makes it uniquely accessible -- you can drop it off at any pharmacy or one-hour lab and get B&W images back.
shooting_tips: Incredibly flexible with exposure -- can be rated from ISO 50 to 800 on the same roll and developed normally in C-41. Overexpose for finer grain and smoother tones. The negatives have an amber/orange base like color film, which affects scanning. For the best B&W prints, ask for hand printing rather than machine prints. Great travel film when you're not sure about lab access.
grain: Very fine -- dye cloud structure rather than silver grain
latitude: Exceptional -- rated from ISO 50 to 800 on one roll
color_palette: Smooth, slightly warm-toned B&W with gentle gradations

name: JCH StreetPan 400
description: High-contrast B&W film originally designed for surveillance cameras, adapted for creative use by Japan Camera Hunter. Distinctively punchy, graphic look with deep blacks and extended red sensitivity for striking skin tones.
history: Based on an AGFA Aviphot surveillance film emulsion. Launched in 2016 by Bellamy Hunt of Japan Camera Hunter. One of the first successful examples of a photography blogger creating their own branded film stock.
shooting_tips: Thrives in harsh midday light and strong shadows. Extended red sensitivity gives unusually smooth skin tones. Pushes well to 800 and 1600. Develop in HC-110 Dilution B for punchy results.
grain: Medium with distinctive, slightly industrial texture
contrast: High with deep blacks and crisp highlights
latitude: Moderate -- 2-3 stops, prefers generous exposure
color_palette: Rich blacks, bright highlights, dramatic midtone separation

name: Kentmere Pan 100
description: Budget-friendly, fine-grain B&W film from Harman Technology. Smooth tonal gradation and good sharpness at a lower price than Ilford's mainline offerings. Ideal for learning B&W or high-volume shooting.
history: Originated from the Kentmere company in England's Lake District, acquired by Ilford/Harman in 2007. Manufactured at the same Mobberley factory as Ilford films. An accessible gateway to analog photography.
shooting_tips: Best in bright, even lighting. Rate at box speed or pull to ISO 50 for maximum smoothness. Responds well to yellow and orange filters. Develop in ID-11 or D-76 for classic results.
grain: Fine, well-controlled cubic grain
contrast: Medium with smooth, even tonal curve
latitude: Moderate -- about 2 stops, best when exposed accurately
color_palette: Clean neutral blacks and whites

name: Kentmere Pan 400
description: Versatile, budget-friendly ISO 400 B&W all-rounder. Classic cubic grain look with moderate grain and good contrast. Often recommended as a first B&W film for newcomers to analog photography.
history: Produced at the Mobberley factory alongside Ilford films. Reformulated after Harman acquisition while maintaining affordable pricing. One of the most popular entry-level B&W films worldwide.
shooting_tips: Forgiving at box speed. Can be push-processed to 800-1600 with acceptable results. Yellow filter enhances sky contrast. Develop in Ilfosol 3 for quick results, ID-11 for finer grain.
grain: Moderate, visible cubic grain with texture
latitude: Good -- about 3 stops, tolerates overexposure well
color_palette: Classic B&W tonality with solid blacks

name: Kodak ColorPlus 200
description: Kodak's most affordable film stock, ColorPlus 200 delivers warm, slightly desaturated colors with a vintage feel. It's grainier and less refined than Gold 200, but that's part of its charm -- it produces images that look like they could have been taken decades ago.
history: ColorPlus 200 is Kodak's budget offering, primarily manufactured for markets outside North America. It uses older emulsion technology, which gives it a distinctly vintage character. Despite being the 'economy' option, it has gained a strong following among photographers who appreciate its unpretentious, nostalgic rendering.
shooting_tips: Best in bright daylight. Expect warm, slightly muted colors compared to Gold 200. Overexposure helps smooth out grain. Don't expect the latitude of Portra -- this film prefers well-lit scenes. A great film for casual shooting and experimentation due to its low cost. Results can vary by batch, which adds to its character.
grain: Medium to prominent
latitude: Moderate
color_palette: Warm, slightly muted, nostalgic

name: Kodak Eastman Double-X
description: A legendary black and white motion picture film with a cinematic pedigree stretching back to the 1950s. Eastman Double-X 5222 delivers a classic, old-Hollywood look with rich midtones, deep blacks, and a distinctive grain structure. It has a lower contrast and smoother tonal curve than most still photography B&W films.
history: Introduced by Kodak in 1959 as a motion picture negative film, Double-X has been used in countless iconic films including Raging Bull, Schindler's List, and The Lighthouse. Available to still photographers primarily through specialty retailers who re-spool the motion picture stock.
shooting_tips: Rate at 200-250 for well-exposed negatives in daylight, or push to 400-800 for indoor work. The remjet backing must be removed before or during processing. Standard B&W developers like D-76, HC-110, and Rodinal all produce excellent results.
grain: Medium -- classic, filmic grain structure
contrast: Low to medium -- cinematic tonal curve
latitude: Very good -- cinema film heritage provides wide latitude
color_palette: Rich midtones, deep blacks, smooth highlight roll-off

name: Kodak Ektachrome E100
description: Kodak's legendary slide film, brought back from the dead. Ektachrome E100 delivers clean, neutral-to-slightly-cool color reproduction with fine grain and excellent sharpness. It sits between Fuji's ultra-saturated Velvia and neutral Provia, offering a distinctly 'Kodak' take on slide film with beautifully rendered skin tones.
history: Discontinued in 2012, Ektachrome's return was announced in 2017 with shipping beginning in late 2018. The revival was a landmark moment for analog photography, signaling Kodak's renewed commitment to film. The new emulsion is based on the original but refined with modern manufacturing.
shooting_tips: Exposure must be precise -- bracket if unsure. Slight underexposure by 1/3 stop can enhance saturation. More forgiving than Velvia but still demands careful metering. Can be push-processed 1 stop with acceptable results. Process in E-6 chemistry.
grain: Very fine -- modern T-Grain slide film
latitude: Narrow -- typical of slide film, about 1 stop tolerance
color_palette: Clean, slightly warm, natural with accurate color reproduction

name: Kodak Ektar 100
description: The world's finest-grain color negative film. Ektar 100 delivers hyper-saturated, ultra-vivid colors with virtually no visible grain. It's a landscape and product photographer's dream -- think Velvia-level saturation but with the exposure latitude of a negative film. Reds and blues pop with incredible intensity.
history: Introduced in 2008, Ektar 100 was Kodak's answer to photographers who loved the saturation of slide film but wanted the forgiveness of negative film. Named after Kodak's historic Ektar lens line, it uses the finest-grain color negative emulsion ever created. It quickly became a favorite for landscape, travel, and product photography.
shooting_tips: Meter carefully -- Ektar is less forgiving of overexposure than Portra, and overexposure can lead to oversaturated, unnatural skin tones. Best for landscapes, architecture, and product photography rather than portraits. Shoot at box speed for maximum saturation. In overcast light, colors remain vivid. Exceptional for scanning due to fine grain.
grain: Finest grain of any color negative film
latitude: Good but less than Portra -- meter carefully
color_palette: Ultra-saturated, vivid reds, greens, and blues

name: Kodak Gold 200
description: The quintessential consumer film stock. Kodak Gold 200 is warm, saturated, and nostalgic -- it's the look of family vacations, birthday parties, and summer memories. Recently embraced by a new generation of photographers for its affordable price and unmistakably warm, golden rendering.
history: Kodak Gold has been a consumer staple since the 1980s, evolving through multiple generations. It represents the 'Kodak look' that defined popular photography for decades. In recent years, Gold 200 has experienced a renaissance as film photography has surged in popularity, becoming one of the most accessible entry points for new film shooters.
shooting_tips: Shoot in daylight for the most vibrant results -- this film loves sunshine. Overexposure by 1 stop enhances the warm, golden tones. Grain is noticeable but adds to the nostalgic character. Works great in point-and-shoot cameras. Underexposure leads to muddy shadows, so err toward brighter situations. A fantastic travel and everyday carry film.
grain: Medium -- adds pleasant character
latitude: Good -- prefers overexposure to underexposure
color_palette: Warm, golden, saturated -- classic 'Kodak warm' look

name: Kodak Portra 160
description: The finest-grained member of the Portra family. Portra 160 is the film of choice when you need maximum detail, smoothest skin tones, and the most subtle color rendering. It's a studio and outdoor portrait workhorse that rewards careful metering with stunningly clean images.
history: Evolved from Kodak's Vericolor line, the Portra 160 saw its most recent reformulation in 2010 alongside the rest of the Portra range. The current version uses T-Grain emulsion technology for remarkably fine grain at its speed, making it a favorite for medium and large format photographers who want to make big prints.
shooting_tips: Best in bright, controlled lighting -- studio strobes, sunny days, or golden hour. Overexpose by 1 stop for the creamiest results. Slightly less forgiving of underexposure than Portra 400, so err on the side of more light. Exceptional in medium and large format where grain is virtually invisible. Meter carefully for the most predictable results.
grain: Extremely fine
latitude: Very good -- best overexposed by 1-2 stops
color_palette: Neutral to slightly warm, ultra-clean pastels

name: Kodak Portra 400
description: The gold standard for portrait and wedding photography. Portra 400 delivers exceptionally natural skin tones, fine grain for its speed, and extraordinary exposure latitude. It handles overexposure beautifully, producing creamy pastel tones that have made it the most popular professional color negative film in the world.
history: Portra 400 traces its lineage back to Kodak's Vericolor series from the 1970s. The original Portra 400NC (Natural Color) and 400VC (Vivid Color) were introduced in 1998. In 2010, Kodak merged these into a single Portra 400 emulsion using Vision technology borrowed from their motion picture division, creating what many consider the finest color negative film ever made.
shooting_tips: Overexpose by 1-2 stops for the classic creamy Portra look -- the film handles overexposure remarkably well, producing softer, more pastel colors. Meter for shadows to retain detail. Works beautifully in open shade and golden hour. For punchier colors, shoot at box speed or slightly underexposed. Pairs exceptionally well with medium format cameras.
grain: Very fine for 400 ISO
latitude: Excellent -- easily handles 3+ stops of overexposure
color_palette: Warm, natural skin tones with soft pastels when overexposed

name: Kodak Portra 800
description: The fastest professional portrait film available, Portra 800 excels in low-light situations while maintaining the Portra family's signature skin tones. It has a warmer, slightly grainier character than Portra 400, giving images a distinct editorial quality that many photographers adore.
history: Introduced as Portra 800 in the early 2000s as part of Kodak's professional Portra line. It was reformulated alongside Portra 400 and 160 in 2010 using Kodak's latest emulsion technology, improving grain structure and color accuracy while maintaining its unique warm-toned character.
shooting_tips: Incredible for indoor events, receptions, and low-light street photography. Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother grain and warmer tones. Can be pushed to 1600 with good results for even darker environments. The warm bias works particularly well under tungsten and mixed artificial lighting. In daylight, it produces a distinctive warm glow.
grain: Medium -- visible but pleasing
latitude: Very good -- handles 2+ stops of overexposure well
color_palette: Warm with golden undertones, especially in skin tones

name: Kodak Pro Image 100
description: Kodak Pro Image 100 is a budget-friendly professional-grade color negative film originally marketed in Latin America and Asia. It delivers warm, saturated colors with fine grain and good latitude, making it a popular choice for wedding and portrait photographers seeking a Portra-like look at a lower price.
history: Pro Image 100 has been a staple in Kodak's international lineup for decades, favored in markets where Portra was less accessible. In recent years it has gained a following among film photographers in North America and Europe for its balance of quality and value.
shooting_tips: Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother skin tones and richer colors. Performs well in bright daylight and open shade. Fine grain makes it suitable for medium format when available. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Fine grain for 100 ISO
latitude: Good -- handles overexposure well
color_palette: Warm, natural with slightly saturated colors

name: Kodak T-Max 100
description: The finest-grained black and white film in Kodak's lineup. T-Max 100 uses tabular-grain (T-Grain) technology to deliver extraordinary sharpness and resolution with virtually invisible grain. It produces smooth, luminous tonal gradations that make it the premier choice for fine art printing, studio work, and any application where maximum detail is paramount.
history: Introduced in 1986 alongside T-Max 400 as part of Kodak's revolutionary T-Grain technology launch. T-Max 100 represented a quantum leap in film technology, offering finer grain and higher resolving power than any previous conventional-grain film at its speed. It quickly became the benchmark for technical B&W photography.
shooting_tips: Shoot at box speed for the finest grain and richest tonality. Use T-Max developer for optimal results, or XTOL for slightly warmer tones. Meter carefully -- this film rewards precise exposure but is less forgiving of underexposure than Tri-X. Exceptional in large format.
grain: Extremely fine -- finest grain of any Kodak B&W film
latitude: Good -- best at box speed or slightly overexposed
color_palette: Smooth, luminous tones with excellent highlight and shadow separation

name: Kodak T-Max 400
description: Kodak's modern T-Grain technology B&W film. T-Max 400 offers significantly finer grain than Tri-X at the same speed, with a smoother, more technical look. Where Tri-X is gritty and expressive, T-Max is precise and clinical -- the choice for photographers who prioritize sharpness and detail over character.
history: Launched in 1986 as part of Kodak's revolutionary T-Max line, it introduced tabular-grain (T-Grain) technology that delivered dramatically finer grain than traditional films. While it never surpassed Tri-X in popularity among photojournalists, it found devoted users among studio, portrait, and fine art photographers who valued its technical excellence.
shooting_tips: More demanding to develop than Tri-X -- temperature and timing are critical. Can be pushed to 800 or 1600 with excellent results. Use T-Max developer for finest grain, or XTOL for a slightly warmer tone. Less forgiving of underexposure than Tri-X. Meter carefully and expose generously for the smoothest tones.
grain: Very fine for 400 ISO -- T-Grain technology
latitude: Very good -- responds well to pushing
color_palette: Smooth, even tones with detailed highlights and shadows

name: Kodak T-Max P3200
description: Kodak's ultra-high-speed B&W film designed for shooting in extremely low light. T-Max P3200 uses multi-layered T-Grain technology to achieve usable results from EI 800 to 25000. The 'P' stands for 'push,' reflecting its design philosophy -- it's optimized to be rated and pushed far beyond its base sensitivity.
history: Originally introduced in 1988 and later discontinued, it was brought back by Kodak in 2018 due to renewed demand from the film photography community. Its true base sensitivity is around EI 800-1000, but it's engineered to perform exceptionally when pushed to 3200, 6400, or even 12800.
shooting_tips: Rate at 1600 for finer grain with more shadow detail, or at 3200 for the intended look. Pushable to 6400 and even 12800 for extreme low-light situations. Use T-Max developer or DD-X for best results. Grain is prominent and atmospheric -- embrace it.
grain: Prominent to heavy -- atmospheric and textural
latitude: Good at rated speed, narrower when pushed aggressively
color_palette: Deep blacks, bright highlights, dramatic tonal contrast

name: Kodak Tri-X 400
description: Arguably the most legendary film stock in history. Tri-X has been the choice of photojournalists, street photographers, and fine art photographers for over 70 years. Its distinctive grain, rich tonal range, and incredible pushability make it one of the most versatile and expressive black and white films ever created.
history: First introduced in 1940 as a high-speed sheet film, Tri-X revolutionized photography by making handheld shooting in available light practical. It was the film of choice for legends like Garry Winogrand, Don McCullin, Robert Frank, and countless photojournalists. Despite reformulations over the decades, it retains the essential character that made it iconic.
shooting_tips: Incredibly versatile -- shoot at box speed, pull to 200, or push to 1600 or even 3200 for gritty, high-contrast results. Pushing Tri-X is a rite of passage for film photographers. In Rodinal developer, grain becomes pronounced and dramatic. In D-76 or XTOL, grain is finer and tones are smoother. Meter for shadows and let highlights take care of themselves.
grain: Medium -- classic, pronounced, beautiful
latitude: Exceptional -- handles push/pull beautifully
color_palette: Rich blacks, bright highlights, beautiful midtone separation

name: Kodak Ultramax 400
description: Kodak's all-purpose consumer film delivers punchy, saturated colors with a warm bias. Ultramax 400 is more affordable than Portra but still produces beautiful results. It has a grainier, more contrasty look that many photographers love for its 'vintage' character and bold color rendering.
history: Ultramax 400 replaced Kodak Max in the early 2000s as their premium consumer 400-speed film. While positioned below the professional Portra line, it has developed a cult following among street photographers, travelers, and anyone who loves bold, saturated color. It's one of the most widely available films in the world.
shooting_tips: Versatile in a wide range of lighting. Overexpose by 1 stop for smoother grain and more saturated colors. Works well in point-and-shoot cameras with built-in flash. Colors can shift toward blue-green in shade -- use a warming filter or shoot in direct light for the warmest results. A great everyday film when you don't want to worry about metering.
grain: Medium to prominent
latitude: Good -- forgiving but not as much as Portra
color_palette: Saturated, warm, bold colors with strong blues and reds

name: Kosmo Foto Mono 100
description: Fine-grain panchromatic B&W film created by the Kosmo Foto analog photography blog. Classic, well-controlled tonality with distinctive retro-styled packaging that has become a collector's item.
history: Launched via Kickstarter in 2018 by Stephen Dowling. One of the most successful film Kickstarter campaigns. Manufactured in Europe. One of the first community-driven branded film products.
shooting_tips: Straightforward, well-behaved at box speed. D-76 and ID-11 for classic results, Rodinal at 1:50 for slightly more texture. Yellow or orange filter for landscape sky contrast.
grain: Fine, well-controlled grain with clean tonal transitions
contrast: Medium with balanced, versatile tonal curve
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Clean, classic B&W with neutral tones

name: Lomography Berlin Kino 400
description: Cine-style B&W film delivering bold contrast and dramatic tonal separation inspired by German Expressionist cinema. Deep, rich blacks and bright highlights with pronounced structured grain. Pushes well to 800 or 1600 for even more dramatic results.
history: Part of Lomography's Kino series, paying homage to Berlin's cinematic heritage from Fritz Lang's Metropolis onward. Designed to evoke the high-contrast look of classic European cinema.
shooting_tips: Expose for shadows and let highlights take care of themselves. Push to 800 or 1600 for more dramatic grain and contrast. Red or orange filters dramatically darken skies for graphic tonal separation.
grain: Pronounced, structured grain with gritty, cinematic texture
contrast: High with deep blacks and bright highlights
latitude: Moderate, prefers slight underexposure for dramatic contrast
color_palette: Deep blacks, bright whites, snappy midtones

name: Lomography Color Negative 100
description: Lomography's fine-grained daylight color negative film. Delivers vibrant, saturated colors with a smooth tonal range. Sharp images with minimal grain, well-suited for outdoor and landscape work with the Lomography punchy aesthetic.
history: Introduced as part of Lomography's own-branded film lineup to complement their creative cameras. A staple of their catalog that has gone through subtle refinements while maintaining its signature saturated look.
shooting_tips: Best in bright daylight or open shade. Slight overexposure by half a stop yields richer colors. Use a polarizing filter for maximum color impact. Tripod recommended for golden hour due to the slower speed.
grain: Fine and tight with smooth transitions
contrast: Medium with punchy, saturated color response
latitude: Moderate -- about 2 stops over and 1 under, favoring overexposure
color_palette: Vivid and warm with strong reds, deep blues, and lush greens

name: Lomography Color Negative 400
description: Lomography's versatile all-rounder. Balances saturated color with enough speed for a wide range of conditions. Visible but pleasing grain adds character. Colors are bold and punchy with warm undertones.
history: The workhorse of the Lomography film lineup and their best-selling film. Manufactured to Lomography's specifications with emphasis on accessibility and creative freedom.
shooting_tips: Great everyday film from golden hour through overcast conditions. Overexposure by one stop smooths grain and enriches colors. Handles mixed lighting with interesting color shifts. Set to f/8 at 1/500s in daylight for classic Lomo shooting.
grain: Medium, visible grain with organic texture
latitude: Good -- about 2 stops in either direction, very forgiving
color_palette: Saturated and warm with strong yellows, vivid reds, lively greens

name: Lomography Color Negative 800
description: High-speed color negative film for low-light and fast action. Expressive visible grain gives images a raw, photojournalistic energy. Colors remain saturated even in dim environments with warm tonality that flatters night scenes.
history: Introduced to fill the need for a fast, affordable color film as high-speed stocks from other manufacturers became scarce. One of the few readily available ISO 800 color negative films.
shooting_tips: Excels in low light -- concerts, indoors, after dark without flash. Slight overexposure by half a stop controls grain and keeps colors rich. Embrace the grain for gritty, atmospheric images. Can be pushed to 1600.
grain: Pronounced, expressive grain with gritty quality
contrast: Medium-high, holds up well in low light
latitude: Good, especially toward overexposure; pushable to 1600
color_palette: Warm and saturated with strong amber under tungsten, vivid neons

name: Lomography Earl Grey 100
description: Fine-grained black and white film from Lomography's Kino series. Earl Grey 100 delivers smooth tonality, rich midtones, and a classic B&W look suitable for portraits, street, and landscape. Named after the tea for its refined, balanced character.
history: Part of Lomography's B&W lineup alongside Lady Grey and Berlin Kino. Earl Grey offers a slower, finer-grained alternative for well-lit conditions.
shooting_tips: Best in daylight or bright indoor light. Expose at box speed for fine grain. Pairs well with red or yellow filters for skies and skin tones. Standard B&W development.
grain: Fine, smooth grain with clean tonality
latitude: Moderate -- about 2 stops
color_palette: Classic B&W with smooth greys and deep blacks

name: Lomography Fantôme Kino 8
description: Ultra-slow ISO 8 B&W film producing extraordinary sharpness and virtually invisible grain. Demands bright conditions or long exposures, rewarding patient photographers with almost medium-format detail from 35mm. Long exposures produce silky water and ghosted motion.
history: The most extreme member of Lomography's Kino series. One of the only ISO 8 films available, appealing to fine-art and pinhole photographers.
shooting_tips: Tripod is absolutely essential. Embrace long exposures for motion blur effects. In bright daylight, a typical exposure might be f/8 at 1/30s. Develop in Perceptol or XTOL for maximum resolution.
grain: Virtually grainless -- among the finest grain of any 35mm film
contrast: Medium with exceptionally long, smooth tonal range
latitude: Narrow -- precise exposure rewarded with stunning tonal range
color_palette: Luminous silver tones with ethereal highlights

name: Lomography Lady Grey 400
description: Lomography's accessible B&W film with a gentle, refined tonal range. Smooth midtones and soft highlights with visible but never harsh grain. A romantic, slightly dreamy quality suited to portraits and everyday documentary.
history: Introduced as an approachable entry point into B&W photography, named to evoke elegance and subtlety. One of the most affordable B&W films available.
shooting_tips: Very forgiving of metering errors -- great for simple cameras. Overexpose by one stop for smooth midtones. Develops well in Rodinal at 1:50 for acutance. Shoot through a UV filter for a dreamy, soft look.
grain: Medium, smooth grain with gentle texture
contrast: Medium-low with soft highlights and open shadows
latitude: Wide -- 2-3 stops in either direction, very beginner-friendly
color_palette: Rich silver-grey midtones with creamy highlights

name: Lomography LomoChrome Metropolis
description: Desaturated, cinematic color negative film that shifts colors toward muted greens, teals, and earthy tones. Shootable between ISO 100 and 400. Suppresses reds and warm tones while emphasizing cool, steely hues, evoking film noir and dystopian atmospheres.
history: Launched in 2019 following a successful crowdfunding campaign. Inspired by desaturated teal-and-orange color grading popular in contemporary cinema. Required extensive emulsion engineering for selective color suppression.
shooting_tips: Shoot at ISO 100 for most pronounced desaturation. Urban environments with concrete and glass produce the most striking results. Overexposure by one stop reveals more tonal nuance. Lean into cool-toned scenes for cohesive results.
grain: Fine to medium with smooth, filmic texture
contrast: Medium-low with compressed highlights and flat cinematic curve
latitude: Wide across ISO 100-400 range; handles overexposure gracefully
color_palette: Desaturated teals, muted greens, steely blues, subdued earth tones

name: Lomography LomoChrome Purple
description: Lomography's iconic color-shifting film that transforms greens into purples, blues into greens, and yellows into pinks. Shootable between ISO 100 and 400 with dramatically different color shifts at each speed. One of the most distinctive specialty films on the market.
history: Launched in 2013 after a massively successful Kickstarter that raised over $400,000. Developed as a successor to the discontinued Kodak Aerochrome infrared color film. Has become Lomography's most iconic specialty product.
shooting_tips: Shoot at ISO 100 for subtle lavender or ISO 400 for deep purple. Scenes with abundant green foliage produce the most dramatic transformations. Overcast skies shift toward turquoise. Avoid grey urban environments with little vegetation.
grain: Fine to medium depending on shooting ISO
contrast: Medium with unique tonal curve emphasizing the color shift
latitude: Wide effective latitude due to ISO 100-400 variable range
color_palette: Psychedelic purples replacing greens, turquoise skies, pink-shifted yellows

name: Lomography Potsdam Kino 100
description: Fine-grained cine-inspired B&W film with smooth, elegant tonality and classic cinema aesthetics. Wide tonal range with creamy highlights and detailed shadows. Softer and more refined than Berlin Kino, ideal for portraiture and carefully composed scenes.
history: Part of Lomography's Kino series, named after historic Studio Babelsberg in Potsdam -- the oldest large-scale film studio in the world. Designed to evoke refined studio cinematography.
shooting_tips: Meter for midtones and let the smooth tonal curve handle the rest. Excels in controlled lighting. Development in D-76 or XTOL brings out the best balance of sharpness and smooth tonality.
grain: Very fine, tight grain with exceptional smoothness
contrast: Medium with smooth, graceful tonal curve
latitude: Good -- about 2 stops in either direction
color_palette: Smooth silver-grey tones with creamy highlights

name: ORWO Wolfen NC500
description: New-production color negative film from the revived East German ORWO brand. Unusual ISO 500 speed with distinctive, slightly muted colors and a vintage European aesthetic. One of the very few new color emulsions developed in the 21st century.
history: Part of ORWO's ambitious relaunch. The original Wolfen factory was an Agfa facility that ended up in the Soviet zone after WWII. ORWO was the dominant film brand throughout the Eastern Bloc until reunification.
shooting_tips: Expect a color palette that leans toward desaturated, cool tones with European character. Expose generously and lean into the muted vintage aesthetic. Standard C-41 processing.
grain: Moderate with textured, organic structure
contrast: Medium with soft, gentle tonal curve
latitude: Good -- about 3 stops, responds well to overexposure
color_palette: Muted, slightly desaturated with cool undertones and vintage aesthetic

name: ORWO Wolfen NP100
description: Fine-grain B&W film carrying forward East German photographic tradition. Classic, clean tonality with a distinctly different character from Western films. 'NP' designates negative panchromatic, continuing the original naming convention.
history: Continues ORWO's original naming convention from the East German era. The original NP films were standard throughout East Germany and the Eastern Bloc.
shooting_tips: Best at box speed in good light. D-76 and ID-11 produce smooth results. Rodinal at 1:50 brings out the film's unique personality. Red filter for dramatic landscapes.
grain: Fine with smooth, even structure
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Clean, neutral B&W with well-separated midtones

name: Revolog 460nm
description: Special effects film pre-exposed at 460nm wavelength, producing an overall blue tone cast. Creates ethereal, underwater, or moonlit atmosphere. Named after the specific wavelength of blue light.
history: Takes its name from the blue light wavelength used in pre-exposure. Bridges physics and art in characteristic Revolog style.
shooting_tips: Cool blue cast works well for moody portraits and night scenes. Warm subjects create compelling contrast against the blue. Overexposure produces softer, more pastel blue. Standard C-41.
grain: Fine to moderate from ISO 200 base
contrast: Medium, slightly compressed by blue overlay
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Pervasive blue tone at 460nm wavelength, cool monochromatic feel

name: Revolog Kolor
description: Special effects film with random splashes and patches of vivid color. Unlike Streak's structured lines, Kolor produces organic, painterly washes in unpredictable locations, transforming scenes into watercolor-splashed photographs.
history: Part of Revolog's extensive Vienna-produced effects range. Hand-created small-batch production ensures each roll is unique.
shooting_tips: Simple, uncluttered compositions let the color splashes shine. Shoot at box speed or slightly over. Bold, graphic subjects provide contrast against color washes. Standard C-41.
grain: Fine to moderate from ISO 200 base
contrast: Medium with areas of intense color overlay
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Vivid random patches of bright color in organic, painterly washes

name: Revolog Streak
description: Special effects film pre-exposed with rainbow-colored light streaks across every frame. Prismatic bands of color interact with subjects in unpredictable ways. Psychedelic, celebratory atmosphere.
history: One of Revolog's most popular effects, produced in Vienna. Meticulous pre-exposure creates rainbow patterns. Over 20 different effects available from Revolog.
shooting_tips: Shoot in well-lit conditions. Streaks most visible against darker areas. Slight overexposure keeps the underlying image clear. Standard C-41.
grain: Fine to moderate from ISO 200 base
latitude: Moderate -- about 2-3 stops
color_palette: Rainbow streaks in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet over standard color

name: Rollei Infrared 400
description: True infrared-sensitive B&W film with sensitivity extending to ~820nm. With an IR-pass filter, produces glowing white foliage, dark skies, and dreamlike atmosphere. One of the last true infrared films in production.
history: One of the very few true infrared-sensitive films still manufactured, carrying on a tradition that Kodak and Konica have abandoned. Essential resource for infrared photographers worldwide.
shooting_tips: For classic IR look, use a 720nm or 850nm filter and rate at ISO 6-25. Load/unload in subdued light. Autofocus won't work reliably -- use manual focus with IR index marks. Without a filter, shoots like normal ISO 400.
grain: Medium, becomes more pronounced with IR filter speed loss
contrast: High when used with infrared filters
latitude: Narrow in IR mode; more forgiving without filters
color_palette: Glowing whites from vegetation, jet-black skies, ethereal halos

name: Rollei Retro 400S
description: High-speed B&W film with extended red sensitivity, combining ISO 400 versatility with the distinctive Retro series tonal rendering. Can produce near-IR effects with red filters while remaining practical for handheld shooting.
history: The fast companion to Retro 80S. Draws on the same heritage of aerial photography emulsions. Offers the Retro look at an everyday-usable speed.
shooting_tips: Without filters, subtly brightens foliage and darkens skies. With red 25A filter, rate at ISO 50-100 for strong near-IR effect. Pushes well to 800. Develop in XTOL at 1:1 for smoothest grain.
grain: Medium with visible texture
latitude: Good -- about 2 stops; pushes to 800
color_palette: Rich silver tones with red-enhanced rendering

name: Rollei Retro 80S
description: Fine-grained B&W film with extended red sensitivity capable of near-infrared effects with filters. The 'S' stands for special sensitization -- vegetation renders lighter, skies darker than standard panchromatic films.
history: Part of the Rollei Retro series, inspired by aerial and surveillance photography emulsions. Bridges the gap between conventional and infrared photography.
shooting_tips: Without filters, an excellent conventional ISO 80 stock. With red 25A filter, rate at ISO 12-25 for near-IR look. Deep orange filter at ISO 25-40 gives milder effect.
grain: Very fine with excellent sharpness and acutance
latitude: Moderate -- careful exposure maximizes spectral characteristics
color_palette: Rich silver tones with enhanced red-channel separation

name: Rollei RPX 100
